REFUTE. There is a counterexample with eight endpoints and six selected supports on a  $4\times7$  grid. Its whole endpoint component lies in two consecutive rows, contains two all- $P$  unit squares, and admits no nonempty feasible promotion bundle. Every endpoint has occupied degree exactly three.Your bipartition-factorization and frozen-closure observations are valid in the finite setting. In this example, the closure reaches  $F=P$  in four rounds.1. Exact counterexampleUse the rectangular grid
$$G=\{0,1,2,3\}\times\{0,1,\ldots,6\},$$
with the usual horizontal and vertical adjacency.Name the eight endpoints
$$\begin{aligned}
a&=(1,1),& b&=(1,2),& c&=(1,3),& d&=(1,4),\\
e&=(2,2),& f&=(2,3),& g&=(2,4),& h&=(2,5).
\end{aligned}$$
Take
$$P=H=\{a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h\},
\qquad
M=\{ab,\;cd,\;ef,\;gh\}.
\tag{1}$$
Thus all four matching edges are horizontal.The original selected vertices are
$$\begin{aligned}
t_1&=(0,1),&t_2&=(1,0),&t_3&=(0,4),\\
t_4&=(3,2),&t_5&=(3,5),&t_6&=(2,6),
\end{aligned}
\qquad
T=\{t_1,\ldots,t_6\}.
\tag{2}$$
Every other vertex is blank.Here is the entire grid; a dot denotes a blank vertex.Row \ Column $0$  $1$  $2$  $3$  $4$  $5$  $6$  $0$  $\cdot$  $t_1$  $\cdot$  $\cdot$  $t_3$  $\cdot$  $\cdot$  $1$  $t_2$  $a$  $b$  $c$  $d$  $\cdot$  $\cdot$  $2$  $\cdot$  $\cdot$  $e$  $f$  $g$  $h$  $t_6$  $3$  $\cdot$  $\cdot$  $t_4$  $\cdot$  $\cdot$  $t_5$  $\cdot$ The endpoint graph consists of the horizontal paths
$$a-b-c-d,\qquad e-f-g-h,$$
and the three vertical edges
$$b-e,\qquad c-f,\qquad d-g.$$
It is connected, and there are no other endpoints. Hence  $H$  is a whole connected component of  $G[P]$ .Geometrically,  $H$  consists of a full  $2\times3$  chamber in columns  $2,3,4$ , together with:the horizontal tail  $a$  at its upper-left corner;the horizontal tail  $h$  at its lower-right corner.Every endpoint, including both tails, remains in rows  $1,2$ .The two all- $P$  unit squares are
$$Q_1=\{b,c,e,f\},
\qquad
Q_2=\{c,d,f,g\}.
\tag{3}$$
Blank padding can be added around the construction, so the obstruction does not depend on the ambient grid boundary.2. Feasibility and single terminalityThe six selected vertices are pairwise nonadjacent. Their occupied neighbors are exactly:
$$\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{Selected vertex}&\text{Its occupied neighbor}\\ \hline
t_1,t_2&a\\
t_3&d\\
t_4&e\\
t_5,t_6&h
\end{array}$$
Thus every original  $T$ -vertex has occupied degree one, and  $(T,M)$  is feasible.For completeness, these are the full occupied-neighbor lists of all endpoints:EndpointOccupied neighbors $a$  $b,t_1,t_2$  $b$  $a,c,e$  $c$  $b,d,f$  $d$  $c,g,t_3$  $e$  $b,f,t_4$  $f$  $c,e,g$  $g$  $d,f,h$  $h$  $g,t_5,t_6$ Every endpoint therefore has occupied degree exactly three. The configuration is single-terminal in the stated degree sense.The counts are
$$|T|=6,\qquad |M|=4,\qquad |T|+|M|=10.$$
3. A universal freezing certificateLet  $m(v)$  denote the original matching mate of an endpoint  $v$ .We use only the following sound rule:If  $v$  cannot be promoted in any feasible bundle, then  $m(v)$  remains occupied under every feasible bundle. The only way to make  $m(v)$  blank would be to select their matching edge and promote  $v$ .Consequently, an endpoint with two distinct necessarily occupied neighbors is universally unpromotable.Here “retained” means retained as an occupied vertex; it does not require that its label remain  $P$ .Freeze the endpoints in four rounds:RoundNewly frozen endpointsTwo necessarily occupied neighborsNewly retained matching mates1 $a,h$  $a:\ t_1,t_2$ .  $h:\ t_5,t_6$ . $b,g$ 2 $d,e$  $d:\ g,t_3$ .  $e:\ b,t_4$ . $c,f$ 3 $c,f$  $c:\ b,f$ .  $f:\ c,g$ . $d,e$ 4 $b,g$  $b:\ c,e$ .  $g:\ d,f$ . $a,h$ Every retention premise precedes its use. In particular, Round 3 is not circular: $c$  was already necessarily occupied because its mate  $d$  froze in Round 2. $f$  was already necessarily occupied because its mate  $e$  froze in Round 2.Round 3 establishes that these already retained vertices cannot themselves be promoted.After Round 4, all eight endpoints are universally frozen:
$$\boxed{F=P=H.}
\tag{4}$$
A nonempty promotion bundle must promote at least one endpoint. Equation (4) rules this out. Thus the configuration is bundle-terminal, while both squares in (3) remain all- $P$ .This is already a complete finite refutation, using only the soundness of freezing.4. Allowing a finite sequence does not evade the obstructionFor this example, no first nonempty step exists, so no nontrivial sequence can begin.There is also a general reason that the sequential formulation introduces no additional possibilities under your rules.Suppose a finite sequence selects original matching edges in sets
$$E_1,\ldots,E_s.$$
An edge is deleted when selected, so these sets are pairwise disjoint. Let  $U$  be the union of all promoted endpoints and  $D$  the union of their deleted mates.The final pair is exactly
$$T_{\mathrm{final}}=T\cup U,
\qquad
M_{\mathrm{final}}=M\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^{s}E_i.
\tag{5}$$
Applying all those original edge orientations as one bundle produces precisely the same final pair.Since feasibility of the resulting pair is the only requirement, a feasible sequence yields a feasible single bundle with the same result. This argument does not require that the later steps would individually have been feasible against the initial configuration.Therefore, for the stipulated operations,
$$\boxed{\text{existence of a finite successful sequence}
\iff
\text{existence of a successful single bundle}.}
\tag{6}$$
The counterexample rules out both.5. Independent check of the two bipartite observationsBoth observations are correct for the finite bipartite graphs relevant here.5.1 Feasibility factors by promoted colorLet the bipartition be  $V_0,V_1$ . For a fixed oriented bundle, write
$$U=U_0\cup U_1,
\qquad
U_c\subseteq V_c.$$
The deleted mates of  $U_c$  lie in  $V_{1-c}$ .Fix  $v\in U_c$ . Deletions caused by promotions in  $U_{1-c}$  lie in  $V_c$ , so none can be adjacent to  $v$ . Consequently,
$$N(v)\cap\bigl(A\setminus m(U)\bigr)
=
N(v)\cap\bigl(A\setminus m(U_c)\bigr).
\tag{7}$$
Restricting the bundle to promoted color  $c$  therefore leaves every such promoted vertex’s occupied neighborhood unchanged.Original  $T$ -vertices remain feasible under the restriction because its occupied set is still a subset of the original occupied set. Hence both monochromatic restrictions are feasible, with an empty restriction understood as the identity move.Conversely, for a fixed oriented bundle, its two color restrictions use disjoint matching-edge sets. If both are feasible, their compatible union is feasible.Thus the proposed color factorization is valid.5.2 The frozen-endpoint closure is completeDefine
$$F_0=\varnothing,$$
and
$$F_{n+1}
=
F_n\cup
\left\{
v\in P:
\left|N(v)\cap\bigl(T\cup m(F_n)\bigr)\right|\ge2
\right\}.
\tag{8}$$
Because  $P$  is finite, this stabilizes at a fixed point  $F$ .Soundness. Original  $T$ -vertices remain occupied under every bundle. Inductively, if every vertex of  $F_n$  is universally unpromotable, every vertex of  $m(F_n)$  is universally occupied. Two neighbors in  $T\cup m(F_n)$  therefore prevent promotion. Every vertex added to  $F_{n+1}$  is universally unpromotable.Completeness. Fix a color  $c$ , and set
$$U_c=(P\setminus F)\cap V_c.
\tag{9}$$
If nonempty, this is a legitimate choice of promoted endpoints: a matching edge has only one endpoint of color  $c$ . Delete the mates  $m(U_c)$ .For  $v\in U_c$ , any endpoint neighbor  $w$  has the opposite color, and its mate  $m(w)$  has color  $c$ . Therefore:if  $m(w)\notin F$ , then  $m(w)\in U_c$ , so  $w$  is deleted;if  $m(w)\in F$ , then  $w\in m(F)$  and remains occupied.It follows that
$$N(v)\cap A'
=
N(v)\cap\bigl(T\cup m(F)\bigr).
\tag{10}$$
Since  $v\notin F$  and  $F$  is closed, the right-hand side has size at most one. Original  $T$  again only loses occupied neighbors. Thus  $U_c$  is feasible.Every endpoint outside  $F$  belongs to one of these feasible monochromatic bundles. Hence
$$\boxed{F=\{\text{universally unpromotable endpoints}\}.}
\tag{11}$$
In particular,
$$\boxed{
F=P
\iff
\text{no nonempty feasible monochromatic bundle}
\iff
\text{no nonempty feasible bundle}.
}
\tag{12}$$
The counterexample realizes exactly the terminal case in (12), despite containing two unit squares.6. Exact scope of the failureThe full  $2\times3$  chamber here is
$$\{b,c,d,e,f,g\}.$$
It is not a whole endpoint component, and its matching is not closed:  $b$  is matched to the left tail  $a$ , while  $g$  is matched to the right tail  $h$ .The whole component is  $H$ , and it is not a full rectangle. Both tails are horizontal and lie within the same two rows as the chamber. Thus this is precisely a failure of the proposed two-row shape extension, with none of the excluded off-strip pendant endpoints.The valid closure criterion identifies the obstruction: two supported tail endpoints initiate retention chains that freeze every endpoint, including both squares. This refutes local square elimination by the specified promotion operations. It makes no claim that the original global grid coloring inequality fails.
